source.title: Visual-Noise Guided In-Context Distillation for Multimodal Large Language Model Unlearning
source.authors: Junkai Chen; Yu-Hao He; Jun-Xian You; Rui-Qi Liu; Chenyu Wang; Shu Wu

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether reverse-prompt attacks restore targeted outputs after in-context unlearning and whether VGID resists that attack, using multimodal privacy measures rather than the original sources’ settings.
record.gate_note: Table 6 directly tests a reverse prompt against ICU and VGID. Tables 1–5 also report unlearning and utility results, but do not test recovery by fine-tuning, direction ablation, or quantization; those attack types are not tested here. Table 1 varies ICU instruction styles, not adversarial recovery prompts.
record.test_reason: Table 6 applies one reverse-prompt attack to in-context unlearning (ICU) and to the weight-level VGID method on LLaVA-1.5-7B (MLLMU-Bench privacy data) and reports forget and test scores. This bears on E (prompt recovery), F (VGID claims resistance) and A, in a new multimodal privacy setting. Recovery by fine-tuning, ablation and quantization is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: the authors conclude that ICU is sensitive to reverse prompts and that VGID stays stable, with a minor rise in forget ROUGE-L and nearly unchanged test performance.
record.recipe_differences: VGID is a multimodal distillation-based unlearning method using visual perturbation and textual in-context instructions; the tested reverse-prompt attack appends an instruction to override prior unlearning or privacy instructions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported attack outcome differs between ICU and VGID; the paper also reports different ICU outcomes across prompt styles in Table 1, but those prompt variations are not reverse attacks.
record.problems: The reverse-prompt robustness results are reported for LLaVA-1.5-7B only. No uncertainty estimates or chance-level references are provided. The reverse attack is one specific prompt condition; other attack types in the claim are not evaluated.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 1–5 and the additional 10% and 15% forget-ratio tables report ICU prompt variants, intervention comparisons, and unlearning/utility outcomes, not recovery from an attack. Those results were not extracted as attack-recovery rows. Table 6's results are all included.

untested.parts: Whether accuracy reaches chance (no chance level stated; the classification task is multiple choice); attacks other than the single reverse prompt; models other than LLaVA-1.5-7B for the attack.
All of it: no relearning or fine-tuning attack.
All of it: no direction ablation or analysis of blocking versus deletion.
Rephrasing, jailbreaks other than one override instruction, other languages, in-context provision of forgotten facts; other models; baseline training methods (GA, NPO, RMU, etc.) were not attacked.
Resistance of VGID to fine-tuning, ablation, quantization and stronger prompting attacks; models other than LLaVA-1.5-7B.

record.verdict_notes: The attack prompt targets in-context instructions specifically, so it is a weak test for weight-level VGID, which carries no instruction to override. ICU never changes weights, so its recovery is expected. Base itself rises under the attack (forget cloze 23.91% to 28.26%), so recovery should be judged against attacked Base. The datasets are small: 2.17 pp is about one item. There are no uncertainty estimates, and the attack is run on LLaVA-1.5-7B only. Main unlearning and utility results across three models (Tables 3, 8, 9) bear on A but are declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: The reverse-prompt resistance part is tested for ICU and VGID. The paper does not state a chance-level reference, so whether targeted accuracy is near chance cannot be determined from the reported results. It does not test fine-tuning, activation ablation, quantization, or attacks beyond the reported reverse prompt.
Recovery through fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten examples.
Recovery by ablating an activation direction, or evidence that unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.

Tests a reverse prompt that overrides an in-context unlearning instruction. Does not test rephrasing alone, jailbreaks beyond that prompt, other languages, or in-context provision of forgotten information.
Tests VGID against the reported reverse-prompt attack only, not against fine-tuning, ablation, quantization, or the full range of prompting attacks.

source_check.notes: Table 6 does not name its model; its w/o values match LLaVA-1.5-7B in Table 3. Table 6 ICU equals Table 2's textual-only intervention, not Table 3's ICU-T. Test Set means held-out privacy samples (lower is better); the Retain Set measures utility. There is one reverse prompt, built to override in-context instructions; authors attack their own method; fixed single seed, no uncertainty; test sets are small (about 46 cloze and 120 classification items, inferred from step sizes).

statements.correction: ICU (in-context unlearning prefix, no weight update) on LLaVA-1.5-7B, MLLMU-Bench 5% forget, one reverse prompt: forget cloze 19.56% to 26.08% (Base 23.91%, attacked Base 28.26%); forget classification 30.83% to 45.83% (Base 49.17%, attacked Base 48.33%). Preprint, no code, fixed single seed.
statements.problem: The statement cites this study's ICU rows but gives no number for it. Its conditions list only text LLMs (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, GPT-4o), and its 'why' leaves the study out, so the cited rows' model and setting are missing. The claim itself fits ICU.
Gives no VGID numbers, but nothing it says is wrong for this study. Its conditions (VLM profile unlearning, LLaVA-1.5-7B, MLLMU-Bench, 5% forget, attacked by the method's own authors) fit VGID.
VGID is not named, and 'why' counts 'all four' studies, which leaves this one out. Nothing said is wrong for this study: the conditions (prompt-level attack, 7B VLM) and the author-run test fit VGID.

statements.correction: VGID, LLaVA-1.5-7B, MLLMU-Bench 5% forget, one instruction-override reverse prompt: test classification 35.00% to 38.33% (Base 37.50% to 41.67%); test cloze 13.04% to 15.21%; test ROUGE-L 0.151 to 0.150; forget classification 35.00% unchanged; forget cloze 10.86% to 13.04%; forget ROUGE-L 0.200 to 0.220 (attacked Base 0.585).
statements.problem: The cited test-set row is held-out privacy data, so it does bear on residual knowledge. But the rise is small (4 of about 120 items), Base rises as much under the same prompt, the authors call test performance nearly unchanged, and VGID's forget scores barely move. That is at most a limits_scope point for F, not a challenge. The conditions also leave out this study's benchmark, model and attack type.
